title: Alike and different: how children get features from their parents

summary.text: Peas from one pod are all green and round, like every pea from that plant. Yet no two of them are the same size. Children are like that too. A child gets their kind, and many features, from their parents, and still comes out as someone new. Your child opens pea pods to see what is alike and what is different, then looks at old family photos to find features passed down.
summary.art: A child sitting on a kitchen floor with an open pea pod in one hand and a row of green peas of different sizes on a white sheet, with a grandmother shelling peas beside her.

intro.hook: Hold a pea pod in your hand. Before you open it, guess: are all the peas inside the same?
intro.text: Every person is like other people in many ways. We all have two eyes, a nose and a beating heart. And every person is a little different. Some of your features are like one parent's, some are like your other parent's, and some are all your own. In this unit we open pea pods, the homes of pea plant babies. Then we look at family photos, to see which features children get from their parents.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a closed green pea pod up to the light, so the round shapes of the peas show through the skin.

outcomes: By the end I can say ways I am like other people, and ways I am different.
By the end I can say that children get features from their parents, and name some of mine.
By the end I can say why brothers and sisters do not look exactly the same.
By the end I can open pea pods and say what was alike and what was different about the peas.
By the end I can tell a feature I got from my parents from something that happened to me, like a cut or a haircut.

terms.meaning: Similar means alike in some way.
terms.example: You and your cousin are similar, because you both have curly hair.
terms.art: Two children side by side, both with curly hair, smiling.

terms.meaning: A feature is one part of how a being looks or is, like hair, eyes, ears or the shape of a leaf.
terms.example: Curly hair is a feature. Big brown eyes are a feature. A dimple is a feature.
terms.art: A child's face with three labels pointing at the hair, the eyes and a dimple.

terms.meaning: To inherit a feature is to get it from your parents. You get it before you are born.
terms.example: A girl inherits her curly hair from her family. A kitten inherits her fur colour from her parents.
terms.art: A mother and a daughter laughing, both with the same dimple in the same cheek.

terms.meaning: A pod is the case that holds the seeds of a pea or bean plant.
terms.example: When you press a pea pod along the edge, it splits open, and you see the peas in a row.
terms.art: An open pea pod with six green peas in a row, and one tiny flat green speck at the end.

explanations.concept: We are similar, and we are different
explanations.definition: All people are alike in many ways, and each person is different in some ways.
explanations.description: All people need food, water and air. We all have a heart and a brain. Most of us have two eyes, two ears and ten fingers. That is how we are alike. But look closely: hair can be curly or straight, and noses and ears have many shapes. Even twins who look the same are different in small ways. Humans are animals, and other animals are the same. Every crow on the wall is a crow, and no two crows are exactly alike.
examples: At an Onam lunch, everyone eats from a banana leaf. Every hand that eats has five fingers, but no two hands are the same size.
Your family photo from Pongal or Durga Puja shows many faces. Each face has eyes, a nose and a mouth, and each face is different.
Two street dogs may both be brown, with the same pointed ears, and still have different tails.
explanations.context: This card says that all people are alike in many ways, and that each person is also different.
explanations.art: A row of five children of different heights, skin colours and hair, all holding hands and laughing.

explanations.concept: Children inherit features from both parents
explanations.definition: Children get features from their mother and from their father. This is called inheriting.
explanations.description: A child gets features from both parents before birth. Inside every living being are tiny instructions for how to grow. Scientists call them genes. Half of a child's genes come from the mother, and half from the father. So a child may have the father's eyebrows and the mother's chin. A child can also have a feature that neither parent shows. It may come from a grandparent. It is the same for other animals and for plants.
examples: A girl may have her Amma's dimple and her Appa's thick eyebrows.
A boy with curly hair may have two parents with straight hair, and a grandmother with curls.
A mango stone grows into a mango tree, never a neem tree.
explanations.context: This card says how children get features from their parents.
explanations.art: A mother, a father and a daughter in a row. A dotted line joins the mother's dimple to the girl's dimple, and another joins the father's eyebrows to the girl's eyebrows.

explanations.concept: Why children of the same parents are not the same
explanations.definition: Brothers and sisters each get a different mix of features from their parents, and each grows in their own way.
explanations.description: Two things make children of the same parents different. First, each child gets a different mix of the parents' features. One sister may get Amma's nose, and her brother may get Appa's nose. Second, each child grows in their own place. Peas from one pod are very much alike, because they have the same parent plant. Yet each pea sat in their own spot in the pod, and some may have got more food than others. So they grew to different sizes. Identical twins start from one egg that split in two, and still their fingerprints are different.
examples: In the pod test, all the peas were green and round, but no two were the same size.
Kittens from one mother cat can be black, ginger, white or patchy.
Twin sisters who look the same can have a different number of moles, and different favourite foods.
explanations.context: This card says why brothers and sisters, and peas from one pod, are not exactly the same.
explanations.art: A mother cat lying with four kittens of different colours: one black, one ginger, one white and one patchy.

explanations.concept: A seed carries the parent plant's features
explanations.definition: A seed grows into a plant of the same kind as the parent plant, with many of the parent's features.
explanations.description: A pea is a seed. Inside it is a tiny baby plant and a store of food. When you plant a pea, a pea plant grows. A seed is alive and aware. She senses water and warmth, and starts to grow when the time is right. Some scientists say a plant does this without any awareness. Plants can also have babies from just one parent. Put a cut mint stem in water, and the stem grows roots. The new plant is almost a copy of the parent, because there was only one parent.
examples: Tomato seeds from a red tomato grow into tomato plants.
Farmers in Punjab and in the Kaveri delta save seeds from their best plants to sow next year.
A cut stem of money plant or mint can grow roots in water and become a new plant.
explanations.context: This card says how a seed or a cut stem grows into a plant like the parent.
explanations.art: A pea plant with white flowers and green pods climbing a stick in a pot, with a split pea beside the pot showing the tiny baby plant inside.

agreed.text: Children get features from both of their parents.
agreed.evidence: A monk named Gregor Mendel showed this with pea plants in the 1860s. Since then, scientists have tested it in thousands of plants and animals, including humans. Doctors can now read the genes a child got from each parent.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: children inherit features from both parents.

agreed.text: A living being always comes from parents of the same kind.
agreed.evidence: A pea seed always grows a pea plant, and a cat's kittens always grow into cats. Farmers and gardeners have seen this for thousands of years.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: babies are the same kind as their parents.

agreed.text: No two people are exactly the same, not even identical twins.
agreed.evidence: Identical twins have the same genes, yet their fingerprints are different. Police in India and all over the world use fingerprints to tell people apart.
agreed.context: This card is about what scientists agree on: every person is different.

challenging.claim: A child is a blend of the two parents, like two paints mixed together.
challenging.who: What most people thought until about 1900
challenging.for: Many children do look a bit like each parent, and some are in between their parents in height.
challenging.against: Mendel crossed tall pea plants with short ones. The children were all tall, not medium. In the next generation, short plants came back. Features are passed on whole, and can hide and come back.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that children are a blend of their parents, like mixed paint.

challenging.claim: A child can only look like their mother or their father.
challenging.for: A child gets their genes from their two parents.
challenging.against: A parent can pass on a feature that does not show on the parent. So a child can have the curls of a grandmother, when both parents have straight hair.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that a child's features always show on one parent.

big_questions.q: If you have a grandparent's curls and a parent's eyes, which parts of you are only yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about your thoughts, what you like and what you remember.

big_questions.q: A mint plant grown from a cut stem is almost a copy of the parent. Is the new plant the same being, or someone new?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the two plants live in the same pot, drink the same water and grow the same new leaves.

big_questions.q: Why were the peas in one pod different sizes, if they all came from one plant?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each pea sat in the pod, and how food reached them.

big_questions.q: How can a feature hide in a parent and then show up in a child?
big_questions.hint: Think of the short pea plants a monk named Gregor Mendel grew. They did not show in their children, and came back in the grandchildren.

story.title: Whose Curls?
story.note: Thenu, Kathir, Revathi, Amma, Appa and Ammamma are made up. Peas really do differ in size within one pod, and a child really can have a feature like a grandparent's that neither parent shows.
text: Thenmozhi lived in a flat in Madurai with her Amma, her Appa and her little brother Kathir. Everyone called her Thenu. She was six, and her hair was a mop of tight black curls.

One afternoon at the school gate, her friend Revathi looked at Thenu's Amma. 'Your Amma's hair is long and straight,' said Revathi. 'Your Appa's hair is straight too. So where did your curls come from?'
Thenu did not know. She thought about it all the way home.
At home, Ammamma had come from Thanjavur for a week. She was sitting on the kitchen floor with a big heap of green pea pods and a steel bowl.

'Come and help me shell these for the kurma,' said Ammamma. She pressed a pod along the edge with her thumb. The pod split open with a small pop. Inside lay a row of green peas, sleeping side by side.
Thenu opened a pod too. She tipped the peas onto her palm. 'Ammamma, they are all green and round,' she said. 'But this one is big, and this one is tiny.'

'Yes,' said Ammamma. 'All these peas came from pea plants. Every pea is a child of a pea plant. They are all green and round, like the peas their parent made. But look closely. No two are just the same.'

Kathir found a pod with seven peas. Thenu found one with only four. At the end of one pod was a tiny flat green speck. 'That one did not grow into a pea,' said Ammamma. 'Every pod is a little different.'
Then Thenu remembered Revathi's question. 'Ammamma, Amma has straight hair. Appa has straight hair. Why do I have curls? Am I different from my family?'
Ammamma smiled. She wiped her hands on her sari and went to her bag. She came back with an old photo album with a soft brown cover.
She opened it to a black and white photo. A young woman stood by the steps of a temple tank, laughing. Her hair was a mop of tight curls.
'Who is that?' asked Thenu.
'That is me,' said Ammamma, 'when I was nineteen.'
Thenu stared. Ammamma's hair was short and grey now. But in the photo it was curly, just like Thenu's.

'Children get features from both their parents,' said Ammamma. 'Your Amma got many features from me. Her hair grew straight. But she could still pass my curls on to you. A parent can pass on a feature that does not show on the parent.'
Kathir pushed in to see the photo. 'What did I get?' he asked.
Ammamma looked at him carefully. 'You have your Appa's ears, which stick out a little. And you have your Amma's dimple when you laugh.' Kathir laughed, and there was the dimple.
'And me?' asked Thenu.
Amma had come in to sit with them. 'You have your Appa's thick eyebrows,' said Amma. 'You have my long fingers. And you have Ammamma's curls.'

Thenu looked at the peas on her palm. She looked at Kathir, and at the photo. 'Kathir and I are like peas from one pod,' she said slowly. 'We have the same Amma and Appa. But we got different features from them.'
'That is right,' said Ammamma. 'Every child is a new mix. Nobody before you had your exact mix of features. Nobody after you will have it either.'
The next day, Thenu ran to Revathi at the gate. 'My curls came from my Ammamma!' she said. 'They hid in my Amma, and they came out on me.'
That night the family ate pea kurma with soft idiyappam. Thenu looked at the peas on her plate. Every one was green. Every one was round. And every one was a little different, just like her family.
story.epiphany: Thenu sees that her curls came from her grandmother, through her mother, even though her mother's hair is straight. She works out that she and her brother are like peas from one pod: alike, but each a new mix.
ask: Where did Thenu's curls come from?
How were the peas in one pod alike, and how were they different?
Kathir and Thenu have the same parents. Why do they have different features?
Which feature of yours is like someone else's in your family?
art: A girl with tight black curls at a school gate, talking to her friend, with her mother's long straight hair visible behind them.
A grandmother in a sari sitting on a kitchen floor shelling green pea pods into a steel bowl, with a girl and a small boy beside her.
A black and white photo of a laughing young woman with tight curls by the stone steps of a temple tank, held open in an old album.
A family eating pea kurma and idiyappam from steel plates, the girl looking closely at the peas on her plate.

games.title: Coin Babies: make babies for two Gumbis
games.context: This is a pretend game about inheriting. Two made-up creatures, Amma Gumbi and Appa Gumbi, have babies. For each feature, a coin decides which parent the baby takes after. Then you draw the baby.

items.b: Heads: round ears, like Amma Gumbi. Tails: pointy ears, like Appa Gumbi.
Heads: blue, like Amma Gumbi. Tails: yellow, like Appa Gumbi.
Heads: spots, like Amma Gumbi. Tails: stripes, like Appa Gumbi.
Heads: three eyes, like Amma Gumbi. Tails: two eyes, like Appa Gumbi.
Heads: a curly tail, like Amma Gumbi. Tails: a straight tail, like Appa Gumbi.

printables.title: The two Gumbi parents, to draw on one sheet
items: Amma Gumbi: a blue body with spots, round ears, three eyes and a curly tail.
Appa Gumbi: a yellow body with stripes, pointy ears, two eyes and a straight tail.

printables.title: 4 baby record boxes to cut out
items: Baby 1. Ears: ___  Body colour: ___  Pattern: ___  Eyes: ___  Tail: ___. Draw the baby here.
Baby 2. Ears: ___  Body colour: ___  Pattern: ___  Eyes: ___  Tail: ___. Draw the baby here.
Baby 3. Ears: ___  Body colour: ___  Pattern: ___  Eyes: ___  Tail: ___. Draw the baby here.
Baby 4. Ears: ___  Body colour: ___  Pattern: ___  Eyes: ___  Tail: ___. Draw the baby here.

rules: Draw Amma Gumbi and Appa Gumbi at the top of a sheet.
Put the five feature cards in a pile. You need one coin.
Take the top card. Toss the coin. Read the back of the card to see which feature the baby gets.
Write it on the record sheet. Do all five cards. That is one baby.
Draw the baby and give them a name.
Make four babies. With more children, take turns, and each child makes one baby.
Then put the drawings side by side. Are any two babies the same?

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two made-up round creatures drawn at the top: one blue with spots, round ears, three eyes and a curly tail, one yellow with stripes, pointy ears, two eyes and a straight tail.
setup.caption: 1. Draw Amma Gumbi and Appa Gumbi.

setup.art: A child tossing a one-rupee coin above a small pile of cut paper cards, with a record sheet beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Take a card, toss the coin, and write down what the baby gets.

setup.art: Four different baby creature drawings in a row, each with a different mix of spots or stripes, ears, eyes and tails.
setup.caption: 3. Draw each baby. Compare all four.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the five feature cards. 2. Help your child draw the two Gumbi parents at the top of a sheet.
flow.say: These are two pretend creatures, Amma Gumbi and Appa Gumbi. They are going to have four babies. Each baby gets every feature from one parent or the other.
flow.kid: Meet Amma Gumbi and Appa Gumbi. They will have four babies.
flow.parent: This game is a pretend model. Real children get thousands of features from their parents, and some features mix in more complicated ways. The idea that a baby gets some features from each parent is true.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes a card and tosses the coin. 2. Read the back of the card aloud. 3. Your child writes or draws that feature on the record sheet. 4. Do all five cards, then draw the whole baby.
flow.say: Heads or tails? Heads, so this baby gets round ears, like Amma Gumbi. Next card. Toss again.
flow.kid: Toss the coin. Find out which feature the baby gets. Draw it.

ask.q: Before you toss, can you guess which ears this baby will get?
good: No, the coin decides.
It could be either.

flow.do: 1. Make three more babies the same way. With more children, each child makes a baby in turn. 2. Lay all four drawings in a row. 3. Ask your child to compare them.
flow.say: Look at all four babies. They all have the same Amma and Appa. Are any two babies the same? Does any baby look just like one parent?
flow.kid: Put the babies in a row. Are any two the same?

ask.q: Why are the babies different, when they have the same parents?
good: Each baby got a different mix.
The coin gave each baby different features.

check.q: Four Gumbi babies have the same two parents. What did you find?
options: All four babies were the same
Each baby had a different mix of features
check.why: Each baby got some features from Amma Gumbi and some from Appa Gumbi, but a different mix each time. Brothers and sisters are like that too.

flow.parent: Two babies can come out the same by chance, because the coin decides. If that happens, say so, and toss for two more babies.

games.title: Alike Jump, Different Spin
games.players: 1 or more children and a grown-up
games.context: This is a moving game. The grown-up names two beings or things. The child jumps and says one way they are alike, then spins and says one way they are different.

items.b: Alike: maybe the same eyes or smile. Different: you are smaller, and you are a new mix.
Alike: both green and round. Different: their size.
Alike: both cats, with fur and whiskers. Different: the kitten is small, and may be another colour.
Alike: two eyes, a nose, a mouth. Different: your hair, your height, your voice.

items.f: A mango tree and a mango seedling
items.b: Alike: the same kind of leaves. Different: the seedling is tiny.
Alike: the same face. Different: their fingerprints, and what each one likes.

items.f: Two curry leaves from one stalk
items.b: Alike: the same smell and shape. Different: size, and the exact edge.
Alike: both birds, with wings and feathers. Different: their colour and their call.

items.f: You and your brother, sister or cousin
items.b: Alike: features from the same family. Different: each of you got a different mix.
Alike: four legs, a tail, a wet nose. Different: their colour and their bark.

items.f: A mint plant and her cut stem growing roots
items.b: Alike: almost everything, because the stem has only one parent. Different: the cut stem is younger and smaller.
Alike: five fingers each. Different: one is left and one is right, and their lines differ.
Alike: both birds, with a beak and two legs. Different: the chick has soft fluff.

items.f: You and your Ammamma, Paati, Nani or Dadi
items.b: Alike: maybe your hair, nose or laugh. Different: your age, and your own mix.
Alike: the same colour and taste. Different: their size and their curve.

items.f: An elephant mother and her calf
items.b: Alike: a trunk, big ears, grey skin. Different: the calf is small and has more hair.

rules: Clear a space on the floor.
The grown-up reads a card. With more than one child, take turns.
The child jumps gently and says one way the two are alike.
Then the child spins round once and says one way they are different.
Any true answer counts. The back of each card has ideas.
Play until all the cards are used, or everyone is dizzy.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a small card aloud in a living room while a child jumps up with both feet off the floor.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up reads a card. Jump and say how they are alike.

setup.art: A child spinning round on the spot with arms out, smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Spin and say how they are different.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and mix them. 2. Show your child how to play with the first card.
flow.say: I will read two things. Jump and tell me one way they are alike. Then spin and tell me one way they are different.
flow.kid: Listen to two things. Jump and say how they are alike. Spin and say how they are different.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. Let your child jump, spin and answer each time.
flow.say: Two peas from one pod. Jump! How are they alike? Now spin! How are they different?
flow.kid: Jump: say how they are alike. Spin: say how they are different.

ask.q: Was there any pair with nothing alike at all?
good: No, every pair had something alike.
Even a crow and a pigeon are both birds.

flow.parent: Accept any true answer. If your child gets stuck, read the back of the card as a hint.

flow.do: Ask the last question and let your child think.
flow.say: That was the last card. Think back over all of them.
flow.kid: Was any pair the same in every way?

ask.q: Were any two exactly the same?
good: No, even twins and the two peas were different.
No, everything had something different.

experiments.title: Pod Sisters and Brothers: are the peas in one pod all the same?
experiments.context: In this experiment you open five pea pods. You line up the peas from each pod and draw round them. Then you find out what is the same about the peas, and what is different.
experiments.question: Are the peas from one pod all the same? Does every pod hold the same number of peas?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will all the peas in one pod be the same size? Will every pod hold the same number of peas? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All five pods come from the same bag, so they grew on the same kind of plant. We look at every pea the same way: we line the peas up and draw round each one. We open five pods, not one, because one pod could be unusual.
results_table: Biggest and smallest pea, drawn round

materials.item: 5 fresh green pea pods (pachai pattani, matar) from one bag (not frozen or shelled peas), in the winter months. When peas are not in season, use any 5 fresh bean pods with seeds inside, such as sem or avarakkai: the beans will be alike in colour and different in size.
a sheet of white paper and a pencil
a steel plate for the empty pods
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Guess. Open five pods. Line up the peas, draw round them and count them. Then compare.

experiments.record: Draw the five pods in a row on the paper. Inside each pod, draw round the real peas, and write how many there were.

setup.art: A child's thumbs pressing along the curved edge of a green pea pod, which is splitting open to show a row of peas.
setup.caption: 1. Press along the edge of the pod until it pops open.

setup.art: A row of green peas laid on white paper, with a pencil line drawn round each pea, some circles bigger than others.
setup.caption: 2. Line up the peas in the order they sat. Draw round each one.

setup.art: Five rows of peas on a white sheet, one row for each pod, with a number written at the end of each row.
setup.caption: 3. Make a row for every pod. Count the peas in each row.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the five closed pods. 2. Ask for both guesses, and the reasons. 3. Write the guesses at the top of the paper.
flow.say: These pods grew on pea plants. The peas inside are the plant's seeds, the plant's babies. Will all the peas in one pod be the same size? Will every pod hold the same number? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The peas are the plant's babies. Are they all the same? Guess. Why do you think so?

ask.q: Will all the peas in one pod be the same size?
good: Yes, because they came from one plant.
No, because some peas are always small.

flow.parent: Many children guess that peas from one pod are all the same, because they look alike at first. Any guess is fine. Write it down and say nothing yet.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses along the curved edge of the first pod with both thumbs until the pod splits. 2. Lay the peas on the paper in a line, in the order they sat in the pod. 3. Your child draws round each pea with the pencil.
flow.say: Press here, along the edge. Did you hear the pop? Now put the peas in a row, the way they sat inside. Draw round each one.
flow.kid: Press the edge of the pod. Pop! Put the peas in a row. Draw round each pea.

ask.q: What do you notice about the peas from this pod?
good: They are all green.
One is bigger than the others.

flow.parent: The pod opens most easily along the curved edge. Peas are soft, so hold the pencil lightly when drawing round them.

flow.do: 1. Open the other four pods the same way. 2. Make a new row on the paper for each pod's peas. 3. Count the peas in each row and write the number at the end.
flow.say: Let us count. How many peas did this pod hold? And this one? Are the numbers the same?
flow.kid: Open the other pods. Make a row for each. Count the peas.

ask.q: Did every pod hold the same number of peas?
good: No, one had 5 and one had 8.
No, they were all different.

flow.parent: Look for a tiny flat green speck in a pod. That is a pea that did not grow. Point it out, but count it separately.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to find the biggest and the smallest pea of all. 2. Put them side by side. 3. Then ask your child to look for two peas that are exactly the same. 4. Use the magnifying glass, if you have one.
flow.say: Can you find two peas that are exactly the same? Look at the size, the shape, the colour and any marks. Put them side by side and look very closely.
flow.kid: Find the biggest pea. Find the smallest. Can you find two the same?

ask.q: What is the same about all the peas?
good: They are all green and round.
They are all peas.
Their size.
Some have a dent, and some are paler.

check.q: What did you find about the peas in your pods?
options: They were all exactly the same
They were all green and round, but not the same size
They were all different kinds of seed
check.why: All the peas were the same colour and shape, because they are all pea plant babies. But no two were exactly the same size. If you found two peas that seemed the same, look again with the magnifying glass.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child three things, one at a time. First, what they found. Then, what they saw that shows it. Last, why they think it happened. 2. Then read the explanation cards together.
flow.say: So, are the peas in one pod all the same? What did you see that tells you? Why do you think they are all green and round? Why are they not all the same size?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Why do you think it happened?
flow.parent: A strong answer: the peas are all green and round because they are all babies of pea plants. They are different sizes probably because each pea grew in their own spot and may have got a different share of food. Let your child say it in their own words first. Cook the peas afterwards in a sundal, kurma or poha.

activities.title: Old Photos: which features came from my family?
activities.context: In this activity you look at photos of your family, old and new. You find features that you share with your parents or grandparents.

materials.item: family photos on a phone or in an album: the child, the parents, and grandparents if you have them

schedule.what: Look at family photos. Find features you share. Draw yourself and colour the shared features.

activities.record: A drawing of your face. Colour each feature in the colour of the person you got it from.

setup.art: A mother and a daughter sitting close together looking at an old photo album and a phone, comparing faces.
setup.caption: 1. Look at family photos, old and new.

setup.art: A child's crayon drawing of her own face, with the eyebrows coloured blue, the dimple coloured red and the hair coloured green, and a key at the side.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your face. Colour each feature by the person who shares it.

flow.do: 1. Sit together with the photos. 2. Find a photo of each parent, and of a grandparent if you can. 3. Ask your child to look at one feature at a time. Try the hair, the eyes, the eyebrows, the nose, the ears and the smile.
flow.say: Let us be detectives. Look at a parent's eyebrows in this photo. Now look at yours in the mirror. Are they the same shape? Now let us look at the ears.
flow.kid: Look at the photo. Now look in the mirror. Do you see the same eyebrows? The same ears?

ask.q: Which of your features is like a parent's?
good: My eyes are like my father's.
My smile is like my mother's.

flow.parent: Families are made in many ways. If your child is adopted, or a parent is not in the photos, compare with any relative, or with photos of a cat family with kittens. You can also say plainly that children in a family share a lot that is not in their faces.

flow.do: 1. Look at an old photo of a grandparent when young, if you have one. 2. Ask whether your child has any feature that neither parent has, but a grandparent does.
flow.say: Here is a grandparent when young. Do you see anything of yours in the face? Something your parents don't have?
flow.kid: Look at a grandparent when young. Do you have anything like them?

ask.q: Do you have a feature like a grandparent's?
good: My curly hair is like my grandfather's.
My nose is like my grandmother's.

flow.parent: Not every family finds one. That is fine. The point is to look closely and compare.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws their own face. 2. Pick one colour for each person. 3. Your child colours each shared feature in that person's colour. 4. Leave the features that are all their own in pencil.
flow.say: Choose a colour for each parent. Colour each feature you share with them. Which features are all your own?
flow.kid: Draw your face. Colour the features you share. Which ones are only yours?

ask.q: Did all your features come from one person?
good: No, some from my mother and some from my father.
No, I am a mix.

activities.title: Ask the Elders: who else in the family has it?
activities.context: In this activity your child asks a grandparent or another older relative about one feature in the family. Then your child draws a family line to show who has it.

materials.item: a phone to call a grandparent, aunt or uncle, or a relative at home

schedule.what: Choose a feature. Ask an elder who else in the family has it. Draw the family line.

activities.record: A family line with three rows: grandparents at the top, parents in the middle, children at the bottom. Colour everyone who has the feature.

setup.art: A girl talking to her grandmother on a video call on a phone, pointing at her own curly hair.
setup.caption: 1. Ask an elder who in the family has the feature.

setup.art: A simple drawing of a family line: two grandparents at the top, parents in the middle and two children at the bottom, with some heads coloured in.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the family line. Colour everyone who has it.

flow.do: Help your child choose one feature that is easy to see. Good ones are curly hair, thick eyebrows, a dimple or a round face.
flow.say: Let us choose one feature to follow through our family. Which one shall we choose?
flow.kid: Choose one feature. Curls? A dimple? Thick eyebrows?

flow.do: Your child asks a grandparent or another older relative: who in the family has this feature? Write down the names for your child.
flow.say: Ask your grandparent: who in our family has a dimple? Did anyone have one long ago?
flow.kid: Ask an elder: who in our family has it?
flow.parent: Older relatives often love this question and remember features of people long gone. If no elder can be asked, use the family photos instead.

flow.do: 1. Draw three rows of circles: grandparents, parents, children. 2. Write a name by each circle for your child. 3. Your child colours everyone who has the feature.
flow.say: Colour everyone who has the feature. Does it show in every row? Did it skip anyone?
flow.kid: Colour everyone who has it. Did it skip anyone?

ask.q: Did the feature show on every person in the line?
good: No, my mother doesn't have it, but my grandmother and I do.
Yes, everyone has it.

projects.title: Mint Babies: a plant with only one parent
projects.context: In this project you put stems of mint (pudina) from the vegetable bunch in water. Over about two weeks, the stems grow roots and become new plants. A mint plant grown this way has only one parent.

materials.item: a bunch of mint (pudina) from the vegetable shop

materials.qty: enough to cover the bottom half of the stems

materials.item: a pot of soil, if you have one

schedule.what: Pick 3 fresh stems. Pull off the lower leaves. Stand the stems in a glass of water by a bright window.
Change the water. Look at the bottom of the stems.
Look for white roots. Draw them.
Look at the new leaves. Smell them. Compare them with a fresh leaf from the same bunch. Plant the stems in soil, if you have a pot.

projects.record: Draw the stems on day 1, day 8 and day 14. Show the roots and the new leaves.

setup.art: Three mint stems with their lower leaves pulled off, standing in a clear glass of water on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 1. Stand three mint stems in water by a bright window.

setup.art: The same glass a week later, with thin white roots growing from the bottom of the stems.
setup.caption: 2. After about a week, look for white roots.

flow.do: 1. Pick 3 stems from the bunch with fresh green tops. 2. Pull off the leaves from the bottom half of each stem. 3. Stand them in the glass with water up to halfway. 4. Put the glass by a bright window, out of strong afternoon sun.
flow.say: This mint stem came from one mint plant. Let us see if a stem can grow into a whole new plant. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Pull off the bottom leaves. Put the stems in water. What will happen?
flow.parent: Mint from the market usually roots in water within one to two weeks. Leaves under the water rot, so keep them above it.

flow.do: 1. Pour out the old water. 2. Pour in fresh water. 3. Look closely at the bottom of the stems.
flow.say: Fresh water keeps the stems healthy. Can you see anything new at the bottom?
flow.kid: Change the water. Look at the bottom of the stems.

flow.do: Look for thin white roots on the stems. Your child draws them.
flow.say: Look! White roots. The stem is growing into a new plant. Who is this new plant's parent?
flow.kid: Look for white roots. Draw them.

ask.q: How many parents does this new mint plant have?
good: One, the mint plant the stem came from.

flow.parent: If no roots show by day 10, the stems may have been old. Try again with a fresh bunch.

flow.do: 1. Look at the new leaves. 2. Rub one leaf and smell it. 3. Compare it with a leaf from the same bunch. 4. Plant the rooted stems in soil, if you have a pot.
flow.say: Smell this new leaf. Does it smell like mint? A plant grown from a stem has only one parent. So the new plant is almost a copy of that parent.
flow.kid: Smell the new leaf. Is it like the parent's leaf? If you have a pot, plant the stems in soil.

ask.q: Why is the new mint plant so like the parent?
good: The new plant has only one parent.
The new plant grew from a part of the parent.

challenges.title: Design Three Babies
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You draw two pretend parent creatures, Amma Starfish-Bird and Appa Starfish-Bird. Then you design three babies, so that each baby clearly comes from both parents and no two babies are the same.
challenges.problem: Design three babies for Amma Starfish-Bird and Appa Starfish-Bird. Each baby must have features from both parents. No two babies may be the same.
constraints: Every baby has at least one feature from each parent.
No two babies are the same.
Each baby is the same kind of creature as the parents.
materials: scissors and old magazines, if you want to cut and stick
general: Make a list of each parent's features first. Your grown-up can write it for you. Then pick some from each list for every baby.
Give the first baby most features from Amma, the second most from Appa, and the third two from each.
Draw the parents along the top and the babies below, with lines from each feature to the parent it came from.
creative: Give one baby a feature from a grandparent, which neither parent shows. Draw the grandparent too.
Make the babies grow up: draw one of them as a grown-up with babies of their own.
Cut feature shapes from paper so you can swap them around to make many more babies.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own two parent creatures, and design three babies for them. Ask someone to guess which feature came from which parent.

setup.art: Two made-up creatures drawn at the top of a sheet: one star-shaped orange bird with long legs and a crest, one purple round bird with short legs and big wings.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the two parents and list their features.

setup.art: Three made-up baby creatures in a row under the parents, each with a different mix of crest, wings, colour and legs, joined by dotted lines to the parents.
setup.caption: 2. Draw three babies with lines to the parents.

flow.do: 1. Draw the two parents together with your child. 2. Amma Starfish-Bird: orange, star-shaped, long legs, a crest on her head. 3. Appa Starfish-Bird: purple, round, short legs, big wings.
flow.say: These are two pretend parents. Let us list their features. What colour is Amma Starfish-Bird? What does Appa have that Amma does not?
flow.kid: Draw the two parents. Say each one's features.

flow.do: Your child designs and draws three babies, choosing features from both parents for each one.
flow.say: Which features will this baby get from Amma? Which from Appa? Remember, no two babies can be the same.
flow.kid: Draw three babies. Give each one features from both parents.
flow.parent: Let your child decide. If they draw a baby just like one parent, ask which feature they could take from the other parent.

flow.do: Check the three rules together, one by one.
flow.say: Does every baby have something from Amma and from Appa? Are any two babies the same? Are they all Starfish-Birds?
flow.kid: Check: something from each parent? No two the same?

ask.q: How did you make sure no two babies were the same?
good: I gave each one a different mix.
I changed the legs and the colour.

items.p: Draw a line from each seed or baby to the grown-up they will become.
items.why: Every seed and every baby grows into the same kind of being as their parents.
items.art: Four pictures on the left (a mango stone, a chick, a pea, a puppy) and four on the right in a mixed order (a dog, a pea plant, a mango tree, a hen).

items.p: Draw the peas from one of your pods in a row. Make each pea the size it really was.
items.a: A row of peas of different sizes, all round.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the peas from one pod were all round, but not all the same size.

items.p: Two peas from the same pod are always exactly the same size.
items.why: False. Each pea grows in their own spot in the pod, and may get a different share of food. So they grow to different sizes.

items.p: A child gets features from only one parent.
items.why: False. A child gets features from both parents, so a child can have a dimple from one parent and thick eyebrows from the other.

items.p: Colour the features a child can get from their parents. Cross out the things that happen to a child after birth.
items.why: Hair that curls, the shape of the nose, a dimple and skin colour come from the parents. A cut and a haircut happen after birth, and a child cannot pass them on.
items.art: Six small pictures: curly hair, a nose, a plaster on a knee, a dimple, a child in a barber's chair, and two hands of different skin colours.

items.p: Circle the one that a child does NOT get from their parents.
opts: The colour of the eyes
Hair that curls
A plaster on a finger
The shape of the ears
items.why: A plaster goes on after a cut. Eye colour, curly hair and ear shape are features a child inherits.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Name one feature you have like someone in your family. Who else has it?
items.a: Any true feature and person, for example: my curly hair is like my grandmother's.
items.why: A strong answer names a real feature and the family member who shares it.

items.p: Kavya and Lalitha, two sisters in Kochi, look at their new baby cousin, Siddharth.

views.says: He looks just like his Amma. He has her round face.
No, he looks like his Appa. He has his Appa's ears.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Could both girls be right? Then say one thing the other girl noticed.
items.a: Both can be right. A baby gets features from both parents, so he can have his Amma's face and his Appa's ears.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a child is a mix, and is fair to both girls.

items.p: Here are a girl, her Amma and her Appa. Draw a red ring round a feature the girl shares with Amma. Draw a blue ring round a feature she shares with Appa.
items.a: A red ring round the girl's dimple, which Amma has. A blue ring round the girl's thick eyebrows, which Appa has.
items.why: A strong answer finds a feature from each parent, which shows that the girl inherited features from both.
items.art: Three faces in a row: a mother with a dimple and thin eyebrows, a father with thick eyebrows and no dimple, and a girl with a dimple and thick eyebrows.

items.p: Count the peas in this pod. Do not count the tiny flat speck. Write the number.
items.a: 6 peas, and one tiny flat speck that did not grow.
items.why: There are 6 peas. The tiny speck is a pea that did not grow, so it is counted on its own.
items.art: An open pea pod with six round green peas of slightly different sizes and one tiny flat green speck at the end.

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items: A pea is planted in soil
A pod grows where a flower was
a: A pea is planted in soil
A pod grows where a flower was
items.why: A pea grows into a plant. The plant flowers. Each flower becomes a pod, and new peas grow inside. Each new pea can grow into a pea plant again.
items.art: Four pictures in a mixed order: an open pod with peas, a pea in soil, a pea plant with white flowers, a small green pod on a plant.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Ammu has curly hair. Her Amma and her Appa both have straight hair. Where could Ammu's curls have come from?
items.a: From a grandparent. A parent can pass on a feature that does not show on the parent.
items.why: A strong answer says the curls could come from someone in the family before her parents, passed on through a parent.

items.p: A black mother cat has four kittens. One is black, one ginger, one white and one patchy. What does this show?
opts: Each kitten got a different mix of features from the two parents
Only the black kitten is really her baby
The kittens changed colour after they were born
items.why: Kittens of the same parents get different mixes. All four are her babies, and the colours were not changed after birth.

items.p: A child gets features from both of their ______.
items.why: Half of a child's genes come from the mother and half from the father.

items.p: Gregor Mendel grew pea plants to find out how features are passed from parents to ______.
items.why: Mendel's pea plants showed that features are passed on from parents to their young.

items.p: Meenakshi and Farhana, two girls in Hyderabad, are talking about pea plants.

views.says: If a tall pea plant and a short pea plant have babies, the babies will be medium, like mixing two paints.
The babies might all be tall, or all short.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? How could the girls find out? Then say why the other girl's idea makes sense too.
items.a: Farhana is closer. When Gregor Mendel did this, all the babies were tall. Short plants came back in the next generation. Meenakshi's idea makes sense, because many children look a bit like both parents.
items.why: A strong answer says to grow the seeds and look, and is fair to Meenakshi's idea.

items.p: Which baby is most like a copy of their one parent?
opts: A kitten
A mint plant grown from a cut stem
A human baby
A puppy
items.why: A mint plant grown from a stem has only one parent, so they are almost a copy of the parent. A kitten, a human baby and a puppy each have two parents and get a mix.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. A farmer saves seeds from her best tomato plant. Why does she do that?
items.a: The seeds will grow into tomato plants like the parent, so next year's plants may have the same good features.
items.why: A strong answer says that a seed grows into a plant with many of the parent plant's features.

items.p: Here are the peas from one pod. Write B on the biggest pea and S on the smallest. Write T on the tiny one that did not grow.
items.a: B on the biggest round pea, S on the smallest round pea, T on the flat speck.
items.why: A strong answer looks closely at size, and sees that peas from one pod are not all the same.
items.art: A row of seven peas from one pod in different sizes, with one tiny flat speck at the end.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down. Why did we open five pods, and not just one?
items.a: One pod could be unusual. Five pods show us if the pattern is true for many pods.
items.why: A strong answer says that more pods make the result more trustworthy.

videos.title: Gregor Mendel and his pea plants, explained simply
videos.why: Shows how a monk found out, with pea plants, that features are passed from parents to children.
videos.check: Find a short, accurate animation. Check it says tall and short pea plants gave all tall children, and short came back in the next generation.

videos.title: Pea plants growing, from seed to pod, as a time-lapse
videos.why: Shows a pea becoming a pea plant, and the plant making new pods of peas.
videos.check: Find a real time-lapse of garden peas, not a cartoon. Check it shows flowers turning into pods.

videos.title: Identical twins: alike and different
videos.why: Shows real twins who look the same, and the small ways they differ.
videos.check: Find a calm, accurate clip suitable for a 6-year-old. Check it says identical twins have the same genes but different fingerprints.

quiz.p: Which of these is true for every person in the world?
opts: We all have the same hair
We all need food, water and air
We are all the same height
quiz.why: Every person needs food, water and air. Hair and height are different from person to person.

quiz.p: Gowri and her cousin Ravi were born on the same day. Are they the same in every way?
opts: Yes, in every way
No, they are alike in some ways and different in others
They are different in every way
quiz.why: Gowri and Ravi are both people, with two eyes and a beating heart. But each has their own features. Being born on the same day does not make two people the same.

quiz.p: What does it mean to inherit a feature?
opts: To get it from your parents before you are born
To learn it at school
To buy it at a shop
quiz.why: To inherit a feature is to get it from your parents. You get it before you are born.

quiz.p: Selvi has curly hair, like her Appa. What can we say?
opts: She inherited curly hair from her Appa
She learned to have curly hair
She caught curly hair, like a cold
quiz.why: Curly hair is a feature that children get from their parents.

quiz.p: Ayesha and her sister have the same Amma and Appa. Why do they look different?
opts: Each sister got a different mix of features from their parents
Because one sister is older
Because they eat different food
quiz.why: Children of the same parents each get a different mix of features. Being older or eating different food does not change the shape of a nose.

quiz.p: Pod 1 held 6 peas. Pod 2 held 8 peas. Both came from the same bag. What does this show?
opts: Pods of the same kind can hold different numbers of peas
Pod 2 is not a pea pod
Peas grow after you open the pod
quiz.why: Every pod of the same kind of plant is a little different, so pods hold different numbers of peas.

quiz.p: A girl feeds a crow and a street dog. Which of them are animals?
opts: Only the crow and the dog
The crow, the dog and the girl
Only the dog
quiz.why: Humans are animals too. A girl, a crow and a dog are all animals.

quiz.p: Someone plants a pea in a pot. What will grow?
opts: A pea plant
A mango tree
Any plant at all
quiz.why: A seed grows into the same kind of plant as the parent. A pea grows into a pea plant.

quiz.p: Anu and Annapoorna are identical twins. They look nearly the same. Is anything different about them?
opts: No, nothing at all
Yes, small things, like their fingerprints and what they like
Yes, they have different parents
quiz.why: Identical twins have the same genes and the same parents. Still, their fingerprints are different, and each twin has their own likes.

quiz.p: Rani had her long hair cut short. Will her children be born with short hair because of that?
opts: Yes, they get her short hair
No, a haircut happens after birth and is not passed on
Yes, but only her daughters
quiz.why: A haircut is something that happens to a person after birth. Children get features such as curly hair from their parents, but not a haircut or a cut on the knee.

applications: Farmers save seeds from their best plants to sow next year, because a plant's seeds grow into plants like the parent.
Plant nurseries grow new mango trees by grafting, and new rose and money plants from cut stems, so the new plants have the parent's features.
Doctors ask about the health of a child's parents and grandparents, because some illnesses run in families.
Police use fingerprints to tell people apart, because no two people have the same fingerprints, not even identical twins.

spotted.text: A mother street cat with kittens of different colours, under a parked car or on a wall.
spotted.art: A tabby mother cat on a low wall with three kittens: one black, one ginger and one tabby.

spotted.text: Heaps of green peas or beans at the vegetable market, all alike and none exactly the same.
spotted.art: A vegetable seller's cart piled with green pea pods and broad beans, with a woman choosing some.

spotted.text: A family photo from a wedding, Onam, Bihu or Eid, where cousins share a smile or a nose.
spotted.art: A big family photo on a wall, with grandparents in the middle and cousins around them.

spotted.text: Curry leaves on one stalk, the same shape and smell, but no two the same size.
spotted.art: A stalk of curry leaves on a kitchen counter, with small and large leaves side by side.

open_questions.q: How do the instructions in a seed or a baby turn into the exact shape of a nose or a leaf?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the genes involved. But how they work together to build an exact shape is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why does one child in a family look much more like one parent?
open_questions.why_open: Each child gets half their genes from each parent. Why some faces end up looking more like one side is not fully understood.

open_questions.q: How much of what we like comes from our parents?
open_questions.why_open: Some likes seem to run in families. But families also share food, habits and homes, so it is hard to tell what was inherited and what was learned.

ask_kids: Who in our family has hands like yours?
Look at the cat on our street. Do her kittens look like her?
When we cut a tomato, are all the seeds the same?
What is one way you are like every child in the world?
What is one feature that nobody else in our family has?

jokes.j: What did baby corn say to mama corn?
Why did the girl bring a ladder to look at her family photos?
jokes.a: She heard she came from a family tree!

jokes.j: What did the kitten say when her fur came out the same colour as her Amma's?
What do you call two peas who look exactly alike?
jokes.a: Nobody knows. We never found two!

jokes.j: Why did the mint stem grow roots in the glass?
jokes.a: To put down roots and start a family.

jokes.j: What did one twin say to the other twin?
jokes.a: You look just like me, but I am the one telling this joke.

jokes.j: What did the baby crow get from her parents?
Why did the pea go to the doctor?
jokes.a: The pea was feeling a little green.

maths.problem: Meera, a girl in Class 1, opened 5 pods. They held 6, 8, 5, 8 and 7 peas. Make a tally. Which number came most often?
maths.answer: 8 came most often. Two pods held 8 peas.
maths.explain: 6: one mark. 8: two marks. 5: one mark. 7: one mark. Two pods held 8 peas, so 8 has the most marks. The other numbers came once each.
maths.context: This is about the pod test, where you counted the peas in five pods.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance that pods hold different numbers of peas.

maths.problem: Pod A held 8 peas. Pod B held 5 peas. How many more peas did pod A hold?
maths.explain: 8 take away 5 leaves 3. Both pods came from the same kind of plant, yet one held 3 more peas.
maths.context: This is about the pod test, where you counted the peas in each pod.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much two pods of the same kind can differ.

maths.problem: Lalitha, a girl in Class 1, made 4 Gumbi babies in the Coin Babies game. Baby 1 had 3 eyes, baby 2 had 2 eyes, baby 3 had 2 eyes and baby 4 had 3 eyes. How many babies got Amma Gumbi's 3 eyes?
maths.explain: Baby 1 and baby 4 had 3 eyes, like Amma Gumbi. Baby 2 and baby 3 had 2 eyes, like Appa Gumbi. So half the babies got each parent's eyes this time.
maths.context: This is about the Coin Babies game, where a coin decided which parent each feature came from.
maths.why_maths: Sorting the babies by a feature shows how many got it from each parent.

song.title: A Bit of Amma, a Bit of Appa
song.note: A song about getting a bit from Amma and a bit from Appa.

links.title: Learn.Genetics: the basics of heredity
links.why: For the parent: clear pages and pictures from the University of Utah on how features are passed on.

links.title: Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden
links.why: See the Great Banyan, one tree that has spread into what looks like a small forest, and many plant families.

links.title: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
links.why: Many kinds of trees and flowers, and a glass house with flower shows twice a year.

links.title: Government Botanical Garden
links.why: Hill plants and flowers from many parts of the world.

warmup.a: To get a feature from your parents.

warmup.q: From how many parents does a child get features?
warmup.a: From both parents, the mother and the father.

warmup.q: Are two peas from one pod exactly the same?
warmup.a: No. They are alike in colour and shape, but not in size.

warmup.q: Name one feature you can inherit.
warmup.a: Curly hair, eye colour, a dimple or the shape of the nose.

warmup.q: Name one thing you cannot inherit.
warmup.a: A cut, a scar or a haircut.

warmup.q: Are identical twins the same in every way?
warmup.a: No. Their fingerprints are different, and so are their likes.

founder: the notebook's RNA story says copies of life were 'never 100%' and that each cell carries chromosomes from both parents in pairs. That became the core idea here, at a six-year-old's level: a child gets features from both parents and is never a copy. The Mendel card from the notebook became how_we_found_out. Most of the file's other notes are for older levels.
science: Mendel, G. (1866). Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden. Verhandlungen des naturforschenden Vereines in Brünn 4: 3 to 47. Tall by short crosses gave all tall offspring; short reappeared in about one quarter of the next generation.

Rediscovery of Mendel's work in 1900 by Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak. Edith Rebecca Saunders bred stocks (Matthiola) with William Bateson and confirmed Mendelian inheritance in other plants: Bateson and Saunders, Reports to the Evolution Committee of the Royal Society, 1902.
Garden pea (Pisum sativum) is mostly self-pollinating. Seed size within a pod varies with position and resource supply; unfertilised or aborted ovules show as small flat specks.
Each child receives half of their nuclear genes from each parent; meiosis and recombination give each egg and sperm a different combination, so full siblings differ.
Identical (monozygotic) twins come from one fertilised egg that splits; they share their genes but have different fingerprints.
Mint (Mentha) stem cuttings root readily in water, usually within one to two weeks; plants grown from cuttings are clones of the parent.
Hair form and other visible features are shaped by many genes; a feature can be carried by a parent who does not show it.
Chandogya Upanishad 6.12 (Uddalaka, Shvetaketu and the banyan seed). Thirukkural, chapter 7, couplet 68.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, 3.1 We are similar and 3.2 We are different.

roots.context: We have opened pea pods and looked for features we share with our family. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: All the peas from our pods were round and green, like every pea from that plant. Yet no two peas were the same size, and the pods held different numbers. Children get their kind and many features from their parents. But no two children of the same parents come out the same.
deep_truth.habit: We often say a child is a copy of a parent, or half of one and half of the other. The peas showed that children of one parent share their kind, and each still comes out new.
deep_truth.evidence: In the pod test, every pea was round and green. No two peas were exactly the same size, and the five pods held different numbers of peas.

three.who_am_i: You are a new mix of features from your family. Nobody ever had your exact mix before.
three.what_is_life: Every living being comes from parents of their own kind, and passes features on to their own young.
three.what_is_this_world: Every pea, kitten and child in the world is like their family, and also someone new.

roots.thread: Before you, there were your parents, and their parents, and theirs, going back a very long way. Each of them passed features on to their children. Each child was a new mix, and passed on a new mix again. In this way, one long family of life keeps making new beings, and each one is a new mix.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a tiny banyan seed. Shvetaketu sees nothing inside. Uddalaka tells him that the whole great banyan tree grows from that fine, unseen thing.
teachings.link: A pea looks small and plain. Yet everything needed to grow a whole pea plant, like the parent, is inside that one pea.

teachings.teaching: When children grow wiser than their parents, it brings joy to everyone in the world.
teachings.link: A child is never just a copy of the parents. Each child is someone new, who can become more than anyone before them.

science.text: Each child gets half of their genes from the mother and half from the father. Each child gets a different mix, so brothers and sisters differ.
How genes work together to build the exact shape of a nose or a leaf is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Many biologists explain every feature by genes and the conditions a child grew in. They see the mix each child gets as chance, like shuffling cards. For them, a new mix is just a new arrangement of old genes.

practice.title: Hands of My Family
practice.say: Sit still, and hold your hands in front of you. Look at your fingers, your nails and the lines on your palms. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. These hands grew with features your family passed on to you. Think of a parent, and breathe in. Think of someone in your family who lived long ago, and breathe out. Now look at your hands again. They are a mix that nobody ever had before.
practice.kid: Hold your hands in front of you. Look at your fingers. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Think of a parent. Your hands are a new mix.

ask: Which of your features came from someone who lived long before you were born?
If every child is a new mix, will anyone ever have your exact mix again?
What would you like to ask your oldest relative about the features in your family?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged, looking at her open hands, with faint drawings behind her of a mother, a grandmother and a great-grandmother, each holding up their hands.

how_we_found_out.context: People once thought a child was a blend of the parents, like mixed paint. This card tells the true story of how that idea was shown wrong, with pea plants.
how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, most people thought a child was a blend of the two parents, like two colours of paint mixed together. A tall parent and a short parent should have a child in between. Gregor Mendel was a monk in Brno, a city now in the Czech Republic. He tested this idea with pea plants. From 1856 to 1863, he grew thousands of pea plants in the monastery garden. He put pollen from tall pea plants onto the flowers of short pea plants. If the blending idea was right, the babies would be medium. But every baby plant grew tall. Then he let those tall babies make seeds of their own. In the next generation, about one plant in every four was short again. The shortness had been passed on, hidden, and came back. So features are not mixed like paint. They are passed on whole. Mendel published his work in 1866, but hardly anyone read it. In 1900, other scientists found it again. In England, Edith Saunders bred flowers called stocks and showed that the same rules worked in other plants too.
how_we_found_out.who: Gregor Mendel, a monk in Brno; Edith Rebecca Saunders, a plant scientist in Cambridge, England
how_we_found_out.when: Mendel grew his peas from 1856 to 1863 and published in 1866. His work was found again in 1900, and Saunders published with William Bateson in 1902.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a child is a blend of the two parents, like two paints mixed together. Mendel's tall and short pea plants had all tall babies, not medium ones, and short plants came back in the next generation.
how_we_found_out.art: A monk in a dark robe in a walled garden, gently brushing pollen onto a pea flower, with rows of tall and short pea plants on sticks behind him.

playtest: Walked through as a parent and child in a flat. The pod test needs only five fresh pea or bean pods, paper and a pencil, and the 25 minutes add up; the mint project's 18 minutes and four day-visits match its schedule. I counted every printable (5 feature cards, 2 parents, 4 baby boxes, 16 call cards) and played both games with 2 players and with 4. Fixed: a brand-name creature renamed Gumbi, coin and crayons added to the game materials, a safety line about a bottle that was never used removed, mint compared with the same bunch, the garbled how-we-found-out heading, the unfinished video notes and song note, a file path in the sources, a fourth repeat of the haircut question (now humans are animals), and the claim that pea size comes from food, now said as 'may'.
